questions.question: The unique sequence of amino acids in a protein, determined by the genes in DNA, is called its:
questions.explanation: The primary structure of a protein is its specific linear sequence of amino acids, determined by the genetic code. It is largely responsible for the protein's function, and a large number of genetic diseases arise from abnormalities in this amino acid sequence.
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Primary Structure

questions.question: Which of the following is a correct characteristic of the peptide bond?

options.A: It is highly flexible and freely rotates
options.B: It is rigid and planar, with partial double-bond character, generally existing in the trans configuration
options.C: It cannot participate in hydrogen bonding
options.D: It only forms between two acidic amino acids

questions.explanation: The peptide bond (C=O to N-H) has partial double-bond character, which makes it rigid and planar rather than freely rotating, and it generally exists in the trans configuration. Both the C=O and N-H groups are polar and participate in hydrogen bond formation, which is important for secondary structure.
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Peptide Bond

questions.question: By convention, when writing a peptide chain, which end is placed on the left?
questions.explanation: Peptide chains are conventionally written with the N-terminal residue (free amino end) on the left and the C-terminal residue (free carboxyl end) on the right; the sequence is read from N-terminal to C-terminal, matching the direction protein biosynthesis proceeds in.
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Peptide Bond

questions.question: A dipeptide, formed from two amino acids, contains how many peptide bonds?
questions.explanation: A dipeptide has two amino acids joined by exactly one peptide bond — a common point of confusion, since it's easy to assume 'two amino acids' implies 'two bonds.'
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Peptide Bond

questions.question: Edman's reagent (phenylisothiocyanate) is used in protein sequencing chiefly because it allows:

options.A: Complete hydrolysis of the protein into free amino acids only
options.B: Selective labelling and removal of the N-terminal amino acid as a PTH-derivative, leaving the rest of the polypeptide intact for repeated cycles
options.C: Cleavage of the protein only at cysteine residues
options.D: Permanent, irreversible denaturation of all peptide bonds

questions.explanation: Unlike Sanger's reagent (which labels and then requires full hydrolysis, destroying the polypeptide), Edman's reagent selectively removes and identifies the N-terminal amino acid as a phenylthiohydantoin (PTH) derivative while leaving the remaining polypeptide intact — allowing the process to be repeated cycle after cycle to read the sequence progressively.
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Determination of Primary Structure

questions.question: What is the key limitation of Sanger's reagent (1-fluoro-2,4-dinitrobenzene) compared to Edman's reagent for determining a protein's amino acid sequence?

options.A: It only works on carbohydrates, not proteins
options.B: After labelling the N-terminal residue, the protein must be fully hydrolysed to identify it — destroying the polypeptide and preventing repeated sequencing cycles
options.C: It cannot label any amino acid at all
options.D: It is more expensive but otherwise functionally identical to Edman's reagent

questions.explanation: Sanger's reagent labels the free N-terminal amino group, but identifying that labelled residue requires complete hydrolysis of the protein — destroying it in the process. This makes it useful only for identifying the N-terminal residue once, unlike Edman degradation which can be repeated.
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Determination of Primary Structure

questions.question: Which enzyme is most commonly used to cleave polypeptides into smaller fragments during sequence determination, due to its well-characterised cleavage specificity?
questions.explanation: Among the proteolytic enzymes with defined specificity for particular peptide bonds (trypsin, chymotrypsin, pepsin, elastase), trypsin is the most commonly used for generating predictable peptide fragments during sequence analysis.
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Determination of Primary Structure

questions.question: Pronase is distinct from enzymes like trypsin or chymotrypsin in protein chemistry because it:

options.A: Is a single enzyme with very narrow specificity for one bond
options.B: Is a mixture of non-specific proteolytic enzymes that causes complete hydrolysis of a protein down to free amino acids
options.C: Only cleaves carbohydrate-protein bonds in glycoproteins
options.D: Cannot hydrolyse peptide bonds at all

questions.explanation: Pronase is a mixture of non-specific proteolytic enzymes that, unlike the more selective trypsin/chymotrypsin/pepsin/elastase, causes complete hydrolysis of a protein all the way down to its free amino acids — useful for determining total amino acid composition rather than sequence.
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Determination of Primary Structure

questions.question: To determine the amino acid composition of a protein, it is first completely hydrolysed. Which method of hydrolysis tends to yield smaller peptides rather than fully free amino acids?
questions.explanation: While acid or alkali treatment can fully hydrolyse a protein down to free amino acids, treatment with enzymes typically results in smaller peptides rather than complete breakdown to individual amino acids, since most proteolytic enzymes have some bond specificity.
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Determination of Primary Structure

questions.question: When naming a peptide, the amino acid suffixes (e.g. '-ine' in glycine) are changed to '-yl' for every residue EXCEPT which one?

options.C: Any residue in the middle of the chain

questions.explanation: In peptide nomenclature, every amino acid's suffix is changed to '-yl' except the C-terminal residue, which keeps its normal name. For example, a tripeptide of glutamate-cysteine-glycine (glycine being C-terminal) is named glutamyl-cysteinyl-glycine.
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Peptide Bond

questions.question: A peptide containing more than 10 amino acids is generally referred to as a:
questions.explanation: Peptides containing more than 10 amino acids (starting around the decapeptide range) are generally referred to as polypeptides.
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Peptide Bond

questions.question: Vitamin B6 collectively refers to which three related pyridine-derivative compounds?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B6 collectively represents three related pyridine-derivative compounds — pyridoxine (a primary alcohol form), pyridoxal (an aldehyde form), and pyridoxamine (an amine form) — which can interconvert, and are together known as the vitamers of B6.

questions.question: The active coenzyme form of Vitamin B6, closely associated with amino acid metabolism, is:
questions.explanation: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) is the active coenzyme form of vitamin B6, found attached to the epsilon-amino group of lysine in enzymes, and is closely associated with amino acid metabolism — participating in transamination, decarboxylation, deamination, and transsulfuration reactions.

questions.question: PLP-dependent decarboxylation of glutamate produces which inhibitory neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation: Glutamate undergoes PLP-dependent decarboxylation to form GABA (gamma-amino butyric acid), which inhibits nerve impulse transmission and is therefore classified as an inhibitory neurotransmitter — distinct from serotonin (from tryptophan) and histamine (from histidine), which are also PLP-dependent decarboxylation products but are not GABA.

questions.question: Pyridoxal phosphate's role in transamination reactions (converting amino acids to keto acids) means vitamin B6 helps integrate which two areas of metabolism?

options.B: Lipid and nucleic acid metabolism only

questions.explanation: Through transamination, PLP converts amino acids to keto acids (e.g. alanine to pyruvate, aspartate to oxaloacetate), which then enter the citric acid cycle for energy generation — this integrates carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism, making B6 an 'energy releasing' vitamin in this sense.

questions.question: Pyridoxal phosphate is required for the synthesis of delta-aminolevulinic acid, which is the precursor for:
questions.explanation: PLP is required for the synthesis of delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA), the key precursor molecule in the heme biosynthesis pathway — linking vitamin B6 status to haemoglobin production.
